---
title: "How the study works, step by step"
subtitle: "Every step shown with a real example, plus a list of the words used in this report"
---

```{r}
source("_common.R", encoding = "UTF-8")
EX <- "women-advertising"
exq <- questions[questions$id == EX, ]
exf <- function(f) rd(file.path("questions", EX, f))
ann_ex <- annif[annif$question_id == EX, ]
anchors_ex <- exf("anchor_concepts.csv")
labels_ex <- exf("concept_labels.csv")
facets_ex <- exf("facet_terms.csv")
plan_ex <- queries[queries$question_id == EX, ]
rec_ex <- records_all[records_all$question_id == EX, ]
claims_ex <- exf("claims.csv")
```

::: {.in-short}
**In short.** A research question goes through eight steps before it becomes an AI answer:
key words, automatic suggestions, the official thesaurus, three searches, the Finna index,
a check of why each record was found, the AI answer, and a check of the answer's citations.
This page follows one real question through all eight: *`r exq$question`*
:::

## 1. The question and its key words

Each question comes with two to four **key words** chosen by the researcher. They are the
core ideas that must appear in the evidence. In this report they are also called **anchors**.

- Question: *`r exq$question`*
- Key words: **`r gsub(";", "** and **", exq$anchors)`**
- Years: `r ifelse(is.na(exq$years) | exq$years == "", "none given", exq$years)`

## 2. Annif suggests subject words

**Annif** is a tool made by the National Library of Finland. It reads a text and suggests
subject words from the official thesaurus, as a cataloguer would. It gives each suggestion a
**confidence score** between 0 and 1.

We reach Annif through our R package **annif**`r if (!is.na(annif_pkg_ver)) paste0(" (version ", annif_pkg_ver, ")") else ""`, which sends the question to the
public Finto AI service and only reads its answer. Annif's models are retrained from time to
time, so the run records which model answered: `r annif_model_text()`.

We keep a suggestion only if it fits one of our key words. It fits when it is the same idea,
a closely related idea in the thesaurus, or shares the start of a word with it (*advertising*
and *advertisements*). A suggestion that is only a piece of a key word phrase (*Finland* for
*Finland Swedes*) is not added, because it would make the search wider than the idea.
Suggestions that fit none of our words are written down but **not searched**. They show how
the computer would have framed the question differently.

```{r}
x <- ann_ex[order(-ann_ex$score), c("label", "score", "fits", "anchor")]
x$score <- num(x$score, 2)
x$anchor[is.na(x$anchor) | x$anchor == ""] <- "-"
x$fits[x$fits == "added to your word" & !ann_ex$used[order(-ann_ex$score)]] <- "fits, but limit reached"
tbl(x, c("Annif's suggestion", "Confidence", "What we did", "Belongs to key word"))
```

In this example only *`r paste(ann_ex$label[ann_ex$used], collapse = ", ")`* was added.
*women* and *advertising* were already our own words, and the rest did not fit either word.

## 3. The official thesaurus gives the standard names

**YSO** (the General Finnish Ontology) is the national list of subject words that Finnish
libraries, archives and museums use to describe their collections. Each idea has one
**official name** in Finnish, Swedish and English, plus links to wider, narrower and related
ideas. We look ideas up through the **Finto** service.

```{r}
a <- anchors_ex
a$found <- ifelse(is.na(a$uri) | a$uri == "", "no match", sprintf("[%s](%s)", a$prefLabel, a$uri))
a$how <- method_plain(a$match_method)
tbl(a[, c("anchor", "found", "how")], c("Your key word", "Official concept", "How it was found"))
```

```{r}
if (!is.null(labels_ex) && nrow(labels_ex)) {
  w <- reshape(labels_ex[, c("uri", "language", "prefLabel")], idvar = "uri", timevar = "language", direction = "wide")
  names(w) <- sub("prefLabel.", "", names(w), fixed = TRUE)
  w$uri <- sprintf("[link](%s)", w$uri)
  cols <- intersect(c("en", "fi", "sv"), names(w))
  tbl(w[, c(cols, "uri")], c(c(en = "English", fi = "Finnish", sv = "Swedish")[cols], "Thesaurus page"))
}
```

## 4. Building the three searches

Every search word has a source: **you**, **Annif** or **the thesaurus**. Search A uses only
your words, B adds Annif's, and C adds the thesaurus names on top. Words for the same idea are
joined with `OR`; the ideas are joined with `AND`.

```{r}
f <- facets_ex[facets_ex$condition == facets_ex$stage, ]
f$source <- c(anchor = "you", annif = "Annif", finto = "thesaurus")[f$source]
f$stage <- cond_short[f$stage]
tbl(f[, c("anchor", "term", "term_language", "source", "stage")],
    c("Key word", "Search word", "Language", "Came from", "First used in"))
```

```{r}
#| results: asis
for (c in conds) {
  cat(sprintf('<span class="cond cond-%s">%s</span>\n\n<div class="query" style="--c:%s">%s</div>\n\n',
              tolower(substr(c, 1, 1)), cond_long[c], cond_col[c], esc(plan_ex$query[plan_ex$condition == c])))
}
```

## 5. Finna answers

**Finna** is the shared search service of Finnish libraries, archives and museums. For each
search it reports how many records in its whole index match (we call this the
**size of the search**), and returns the best-matching records in its own order. We keep the
**top 60** from each search, so all three searches get the same amount of space.

```{r}
p <- plan_ex[, c("condition", "query_terms", "index_matches", "retrieved")]
p$condition <- cond_short[p$condition]
tbl(p, c("Search", "Search words", "Matching records in Finna", "Records kept (max 60)"))
```

Because each search keeps only 60 records, a wider search does not just **add** records: it
can also **push out** records that a narrower search would have shown.

## 6. Why was each record found?

For every record we look for the search words in its title, subject words and description.
That tells us which step brought it in:

- **your words**: one of your own key words appears;
- **Annif**: it only matches through a word Annif suggested;
- **thesaurus**: it only matches through an official name added in search C (often Finnish or Swedish);
- **hidden**: none of the words is visible in the parts of the record we can see. Finna searches
  more fields than it shows us, so we cannot tell why it matched.

```{r}
t <- table(factor(rec_ex$condition, conds), factor(rec_ex$introduced_by, c("anchor", "annif", "finto", "unobserved")))
t <- as.data.frame.matrix(t)
tbl(data.frame(Search = cond_short, t, check.names = FALSE),
    c("Search", "Your words", "Annif", "Thesaurus", "Hidden"))
```

## 7. The AI writes an answer

The **top 8 records** of each search go to an AI model (here from `r provider_name(run_info$provider)`), with
strict rules: use only these records, say when the evidence is too thin, and put the record
numbers after every sentence that says something about the records. So each search gets its
own answer.

```{r}
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(claims_ex) && nrow(claims_ex)) {
  s <- claims_ex[claims_ex$condition == "A_direct" & claims_ex$has_citation, ]
  s <- head(s[nchar(s$text) < 420, ], 2)
  cat("Two sentences from the answer for search A:\n\n")
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(s))) cat("> ", esc(s$text[i]), "\n\n", sep = "")
} else cat("This run has no AI answers.\n")
```

## 8. Checking the answer

We split every answer into sentences and check, automatically:

- whether the sentence cites any records;
- whether the cited records really were among the 8 the AI received (if not, it made them up);
- which search step brought the cited records in, and whether search A could have found them.

What a computer **cannot** check is whether the records really support what the sentence says.
That is the job of the [human checking](human-check.qmd).

## Words used in this report

::: {.term}
Finna
: The national search service for Finnish libraries, archives and museums. All records in this study come from it.

Annif
: An automatic subject-indexing tool from the National Library of Finland, offered as the public service Finto AI. It suggests subject words for a text. We use it through the R package *annif*.

YSO
: The General Finnish Ontology: the official list of subject words, with names in Finnish, Swedish and English.

Finto
: The online service where YSO and other Finnish vocabularies are published. We use it to look up YSO.

Key word (anchor)
: One of the two to four core ideas the researcher picks for a question, e.g. *women* and *advertising*.

Search A, B, C
: A uses only your key words. B adds Annif's suggestions that fit them. C adds YSO's official names in three languages.

Query
: The exact text sent to Finna. `AND` means both ideas must appear; `OR` means any of the listed words will do.

Matching records (size of the search)
: How many records in the whole Finna index match a search. It shows how wide the search is.

Records kept
: The top 60 records of a search, in Finna's order. All comparisons use these.

Evidence
: The top 8 records that the AI reads before writing its answer.

Overlap
: How many records two searches have in common. We use the **Jaccard** share: records found by both, divided by records found by either. 1 means the same records, 0 means none shared.

Rank overlap (RBO)
: Like overlap, but it cares most about the top of the list. Two searches that agree on their first few records score high even if they differ further down.

Difference in mix (JSD)
: The **Jensen-Shannon divergence**. A number from 0 to 1 that compares two mixes, for example of institutions. 0 = exactly the same mix; 1 = nothing in common. Around 0.1 is a small change; above 0.5 is a big one.

Uncertainty range
: Because we only look at 60 records, a mix could look different just by chance. The range shows the values that are believable given the records we have.

Diversity
: How many different institutions (or languages) a search shows, counting rare ones less. Ten equally common institutions give a diversity of 10.

Hidden match
: A record that matches a search, but none of the search words appear in the parts of the record that Finna shows us.

Claim
: One sentence of an AI answer.

Citation
: A record number in square brackets after a sentence, for example `[werstas.we-1372484]`.

Blinded checking
: The checkers see the records and sentences mixed up, without knowing which search they came from, so their judgement is fair.
:::
